cultivar: Anhua and other Hunan medium- and large-leaf population bushes
processing: Grade-1 Anhua hei mao cha (pan-fired, rolled, briefly pile-fermented and dried over pine fires) is steamed and lightly packed into bamboo baskets lined with bamboo leaves, then stored to dry and mature; it is not pressed hard.
harvest_season: Spring leaf picked around Guyu as a bud with two or three leaves – the most tender material used for any Anhua dark tea.
appearance_dry: Slim, twisted dark-brown leaves with a dull sheen, loose or lightly matted from the basket, smelling of pine smoke.
appearance_liquor: Orange-yellow to amber, clear and bright.
appearance_wet: Dark olive-brown leaves, still whole and relatively tender.
taste_profile: Clean and sweet with pine smoke, dried longan and a light, cooling aged note; the most delicate of the Anhua teas, closer to a smoky aged white tea than to a brick.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, boiling water, short steeps; it does not need simmering but takes it well. A gaiwan shows the pine, a clay pot rounds it.

vintage_note: Sold by year in 1 kg or smaller bamboo baskets and in loose packs; drinkable the year it is made, and the usual market range is 1–15 years, with 2000s baskets common and 1990s or older sold as collector's tea. The pine smoke softens noticeably after 3–5 years.
description:
Tian Jian, 'heavenly tips', is the top of the three 'Jian' grades of Anhua dark tea and the gentlest thing the county makes. It is dark tea from tender spring leaf – a bud with two or three leaves – rather than the coarse summer leaf that goes into bricks, and it is sold loose in bamboo baskets rather than pressed, which is why it looks and brews more like a smoky aged tea than like a block. Local tradition says it was sent as tribute in the Daoguang era, which is the usual explanation of the name and the one below it, Gong Jian ('tribute tips').

The leaf is processed as hei mao cha – pan-fired, rolled, briefly piled and dried over pine wood on the seven-star stove that gives all Anhua tea its smoke – then steamed and packed lightly into baskets lined with bamboo leaves, traditionally large ones and now mostly one-kilo retail baskets, where it dries out and matures. No hard pressing and no golden-flower step: the tea is the leaf, the pine and the years.

In the cup it is clean and sweet, with pine smoke up front, dried longan behind it and a light, cooling note that reads as 'aged' even in young tea; it gives eight or nine steeps with boiling water after a rinse, and because the leaf is tender it is one Anhua tea that does not need simmering. Young Tian Jian is noticeably smoky; after three to five years the smoke settles into the sweetness, which is when most people like it best.

It is sold by year and factory in baskets and loose packs, and it is the most expensive Anhua tea per gram because of the leaf grade. Look for whole, even, slim leaves and a sweet pine smell with no mustiness; stemmy, broken leaf sold as Tian Jian is a lower Jian grade. Baskets breathe and the tea keeps changing, so an older basket from a dry store is worth paying a bit more for.

If Anhua bricks feel too heavy, this is the tea to start with; if you drink smoked Lapsang, it is the dark-tea cousin that will make immediate sense.
sources_note: The tribute-tea origin of the Tian Jian / Gong Jian names is local tradition, presented as such. Traditional basket sizes (large baskets of tens of kilos) versus modern 1 kg retail baskets follow Chinese trade descriptions.
history:
Tian Jian is the top grade of Anhua's basket teas. The family is traced to the Qianlong era, when Shanxi merchants from Quwo and local tea houses took the more tender dark leaf and reprocessed it into lightly pressed baskets. There were once seven named grades; after 1949 three remained, Tian Jian, Gong Jian and Sheng Jian.

The usual story says the Daoguang emperor named it in 1825 and made it an imperial tea. It is a good story, repeated in Anhua, without firm evidence behind it.

The modern record is clearer. In 1967 the name was judged feudal and the tea became Xiang Jian No. 1 at the Baishaxi factory, returning to Tian Jian in 1983. Baishaxi's production criteria fed the industry standard issued in 2010, raised to a national standard in 2016.
